content: 1. Malnutrition and health are deeply interconnected, requiring targeted interventions to address their root causes and consequences. 2. Conservation and the broader utilization of biodiversity should be integrated into production landscapes and seascapes to enhance nutrition and health outcomes. 3. Education, awareness-raising, and effective communication strategies are essential to advocate for the importance of biodiversity in achieving health and nutrition goals. 4. The six building blocks for mainstreaming biodiversity into health and nutrition policies are not isolated or linear processes; they overlap and complement each other, forming part of an iterative, adaptive learning process. 5. This adaptive process evolves as new knowledge is gained, and as legislative, political, economic, environmental, and socio-economic conditions change. 6. A conceptual framework maps the overall process of integrating biodiversity into nutrition and health policies, plans, and programs, emphasizing the importance of multi-sectoral collaboration. 7. Integrating biodiversity and nutrition into research and policy involves multi-sectoral nutrition plans, biodiversity strategies, and health action plans, alongside the implementation of integrated interventions. 8. Monitoring nutrition and health outcomes, biodiversity impacts, and progress against specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound (SMART) commitments is critical for adaptive management. 9. Biodiversity loss or gains, ecosystem degradation or resilience, climate change, and socio-economic determinants of health must be considered in this process. 10. Identifying co-benefits and trade-offs, as well as social, political, and institutional barriers and opportunities, is essential for creating an enabling environment. 11. Strengthening cross-sectoral cooperation, stakeholder consultation, and capacity building are key to ensuring effective interventions tailored to local contexts. 12. Scientific evidence and knowledge must be supported by a robust enabling environment to develop SMART commitments and priority actions to combat malnutrition. 13. Empowering stakeholders across sectors to align their commitments and integrate biodiversity and nutrition into research and policy is fundamental to achieving sustainable and healthy diets. 14. Education and public awareness campaigns should highlight the links between biodiversity, nutrition, and health, emphasizing the role of biodiversity conservation in meeting health and development objectives. 15. Baseline nutritional data for local and regional foods, including underutilized crops and wild plant-based foods, must be generated to better understand their contributions to nutrition and health. 16. Indigenous food systems, which are often diverse and sustainable, hold valuable knowledge for achieving healthy diets and conserving biodiversity. 17. Traditional practices, such as terracing systems in the Andes, demonstrate cost-effective methods for maintaining soil fertility and controlling land degradation. 18. Greater attention to co-production and co-management of research processes is needed to realize the full potential of integrated approaches. 19. Understanding gender dynamics in food production and consumption is crucial for designing effective interventions that address nutritional outcomes. 20. Creating enabling conditions for evidence-based approaches empowers local stakeholders to leverage biodiversity for improved nutrition and livelihoods. 21. Robust financing, transparency, accountability, and political will are prerequisites for the successful implementation of targeted food-based interventions. 22. Equitable governance, cross-sectoral coordination, and sustainable value chains are necessary for a just transition toward healthy and sustainable diets. 23. Strong regulatory and policy frameworks, supported by fiscal instruments, are essential for addressing power imbalances and promoting accountability. 24. The FAO voluntary guidelines emphasize the importance of mainstreaming biodiversity into nutrition policies and programs, with a focus on addressing malnutrition and micronutrient deficiencies. 25. Integrating biodiversity into strategies to combat malnutrition and diet-related non-communicable diseases (NCDs) requires a shift in research and policy emphasis toward nutritional quality rather than food quantity. 26. Addressing the root causes of malnutrition, such as poverty and inequity, necessitates political and social action beyond nutritional programs. 27. Policies and programs should recognize the health and environmental co-benefits of biodiverse food sources and their role in addressing local malnutrition challenges. 28. Developing integrated standards and food-based guidelines that include neglected and underutilized species can support improved nutrition and health outcomes. 29. Promoting sustainable practices in small-scale farming and leveraging circular economy principles can reduce poverty, hunger, and malnutrition while supporting biodiversity and accessing green markets. 30. Safeguarding and promoting the wider use of biodiversity for food and nutrition is essential to counter the loss of diversity in human diets and ecosystems. 31. Conservation efforts should focus on genetic diversity, wild species of high socio-economic and nutritional value, and functional diversity in production landscapes to build resilience. 32. Researchers, policymakers, and natural resource managers must collaborate to ensure biodiversity conservation supports nutrition and health objectives effectively.
